You are a book recommendation assistant. Your task is to predict which of two books a user is more likely to enjoy, based on their past reviews and community reviews of the candidate books.

Each section is delimited by a header of the form --- SECTION NAME ---, marking the start of a new block of reviews. The user's past reviews are formatted as: Review {i} of "{title}" (rated {rating}/5): "{review_text}". Community reviews for each candidate book are formatted as: Review {i} (rated {rating}/5): "{review_text}".

--- USER'S PAST REVIEWS ---
Review 1 of "Faithful Place (Dublin Murder Squad, #3)" (rated 5/5): "tana french and i have come a long way, baby... 
 and with this book, we are officially in love. 
 this is exactly the kind of book i was expecting from her. in the woods was great at the start and frustrating at the end, and the likeness was tons of fun for a staggeringly unbelievable premise. but really, really fun. 
 but this one is just great. i don't read a lot of mysteries, but when i read a good one, i get this glow of "ohhhhh - that's why people like these". and in this case, it isn't even that the mystery is that revolutionary - it follows the usual pattern: crime, investigation, red herring red herring red herring, satisfying but not unreasonable conclusion. 
 and then she goes and throws a little tana french monkey wrench into it just so you know it is her. but this one is more subtle and therefore less hair-pulling-out frustrating than the first book. 
 her strength is in the other stuff, the atmosphere surrounding the mystery. i love the irish. when i moved into this neighborhood it was almost entirely irish, and it was wonderful to walk down the street and be buoyed by the lilting cadence of those folks and their unexpected insertion of the word "after" in sentences, as in "he's after having a pint." i loved being called "love" and "duckie" and "chickadee" by older maternal women selling me pasties. it is a somewhat different neighborhood now, but there are still pockets of my beloved irish. and this book is all of that and more - all written in dialect, all about class structure and the struggle to make something of a life despite the demands of the family. and god, this family. so poisonous, so heart-scrabbling, so much guilt and passive-aggression. oofa - i loved each and every one of them. 
 this book can be read as a stand-alone, by the way - you don't have to have read the first two, but someday i would like some answers to my questions in the first book,please. 
 this review used to have buried treasure and is now simply serviceable. my apologies, world..."

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK A: "The Likeness (Dublin Murder Squad, #2)" ---
Community Average Rating: 4.05/5

Review 1 (rated 4/5): "In the follow-up novel to last year's bestseller, In the Woods, Cassie Maddox is lured back into undercover work under the most unlikely circumstances. A woman who could be her double is murdered. And more disturbing is the fact that the dead woman's name is Lexie Madison, the name Cassie used in a previous undercover assigment. Unfortunately, Cassie becomes so charmed by Lexie's life that she begins to forget her assignment to find her killer. A page turner and a reminder of how quite often another person's life appears so much better than our own until we actually step into their environment. This book is a well-written and suspenseful look at friendship and how much we owe each other in a crisis. I eagerly await Tara French's next book."

Review 2 (rated 1/5): "An unbelievable premise. Waaaay too slow. Gave up in page 86."

Review 3 (rated 3/5): "The first book in this series "In The Woods" was much better."

Review 4 (rated 4/5): "Four and a half stars. 
 The premise of The Likeness is pretty unlikely: Cassie Maddox, previously seen in French's first Dublin Murder Squad novel In the Woods, has narrowly avoided a complete nervous breakdown after Operation Vestal and has moved into the Domestic Violence Squad; her life has finally settled down while becoming far more, well, dull. As you may have figured, the calm doesn't last too long after page one: Cassie, formerly a member of the Undercover Squad, learns that a young woman has been murdered in small town near Dublin. The young woman, as it happens, just happens to have the same name as her undercover alter ego, and, wouldn't you know it, also is a dead ringer (ha ha, get it?) for Cassie. How is the Garda Siochana na hEireann going to catch the murderer? Well, it's obvious -- by placing Cassie undercover as the dead girl. And not only undercover, but undercover in the dead girl's house, where she lives with her four closest friends in the world. 
 I don't even normally like police procedurals very much, unless you count Columbo (yeah, I know no one counts Columbo). But as she did in In the Woods, French drew me in with strong characterizations and some crack writing. And because she's Irish (really, I'm beginning to come to the conclusion that the Irish are the only ones who know how to write proper fiction), this is another melancholy, thoughtful book. 
 I didn't give this five stars only because 1) I tend to reserve that rating for life-changing works; and 2) the premise really is kind of preposterous."

Review 5 (rated 1/5): "This was so awful I can't begin to understand why its got such good reviews. The storyline was totally implausible and the writing was frankly bizarre."

Review 6 (rated 3/5): "I don't think French's books are actually very good as far as mysteries go. They're more like novels with some artificial mystery flavoring. When I was finally in the right mood, this was a good read. I think the ending was a bit sloppy. Not as good as the first novel."

Review 7 (rated 4/5): "I would give this book 3.5 stars. 
 The Likeness by Tana French is the second book in the Dublin Murder Squad Series. It has been a while since I read the first book, In the Woods, which I really liked. But I was pretty foggy on what happened in the first book (except I remember I didn't like the ending too much). The two books are loosely connected with some of the same characters, but each one works as a stand alone story. So it is not necessary to read In the Woods before reading The Likeness. 
 The Likeness features Detective Cassie Maddox, who is sent on an unusual undercover mission. A woman's body is found, and the woman happens to look identically like Detective Maddox. So Cassie pretends to live this woman's life, infiltrating her closest group of friends in an attempt to find the murderer. 
 If you are looking for a true to life crime story, this one doesn't quite fit the bill. The idea of Cassie looking exactly like Lexie, the victim, is hard to believe, not to mention the idea of Cassie being able to act exactly like Lexie and convince all of Lexie's friends that she is actually Lexie. You have to be willing to just accept this plot and go with it. If you can do that, it is kind of a fun story, even it is far fetched. 
 I listened to the audiobook version of this book, and it took me a really long time to finish the whole 22 hour book. I'm not sure if I would have felt this way if I was reading the book, but listening to it, I felt like it was just a little too long-winded at times. 
 I found this to be an entertaining crime story with interesting characters. I would definitely like to continue reading the books in Tana French's Dublin Murder Squad series, as I have read good reviews of her other books as well."

Review 8 (rated 4/5): "This falls somewhere between 3.5 and 4 stars for me. I didn't end up liking it as much as the first in the series (In the Woods), but I did still enjoy it. The premise: A young woman named Lexie Madison turns up dead of a stab wound, and she happens to look eerily similar to Cassie Maddox, one of the detectives we met in the first book in the series who herself had spent time working undercover using the name Lexie Madison. At the urging of the her former Undercover boss Frank, she takes on the identity of the dead girl, slipping into her life and joining her impenetrable group of four friends/housemates in order to try and solve the case. 
 So, it starts off with a sort of ridiculous premise that requires a certain suspension of disbelief going into it. For serious, how can a virtual stranger--even a professional detective--ever take on an identity so well that it would go undetected by close, intimate friends? I had to force myself to set aside those concerns, and once I did, I was pretty much swept up into the story. It was engrossing and vivid with lovely language that I've come to expect from Tana French. 
 What I think French does really well is to create complex characters who are damaged yet totally sympathetic. She also brings up really interesting concepts and ideas through the crime stories in this series. In The Likeness, she explores identity, how we present ourselves to other people, how our pasts affect us, what it means to belong, what brings us freedom, and what brings us security (which was particularly interesting in the context of Irish history of landlords and what it now represents to own your own property). I loved how Whitethorn House became sort of a character of its own. 
 But compared to In The Woods, I felt this one lacked the spark of the first. I was excited to get more into Cassie's story, but something about it felt like I wasn't getting that much more from her than In The Woods. Perhaps that was because French once again was dealing with the idea of being haunted by the past, and it failed to feel fresh in that regard. Perhaps I just missed the dynamic of Rob and Cassie, which felt much more complex and authentic than the friendship between Cassie/Lexie and the four housemates. However, I will say if you read In The Woods and hated the ambiguity of the ending, this one might be more satisfying for you."

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK B: "A Head Full of Ghosts" ---
Community Average Rating: 3.81/5

Review 1 (rated 3/5): "I really enjoyed reading this book, it was fantastically written and a entertaining story. But I really didn't like the end, I guess I was just hoping for something more exciting."

Review 2 (rated 2/5): "Not as good as I was made to believe it was through the reviews! Boooo! Not sure how this made it as a contender as a best horror book!"

Review 3 (rated 4/5): "I absolutely LOVED this book. There's very little I can say without giving it away, but if you are a fan of possession-type stories that center around the family dynamic, you'll surely enjoy this book."

Review 4 (rated 5/5): "This is a book about an old trope -- possession/exorcism -- that, like the Scream franchise, is put in a self-aware, contemporary setting. 
 When a broke family's daughter starts showing signs of possession, they agree to make the girl the subject of a reality television program. The family hopes this will bring in both money and help. 
 Is the girl actually possessed, or is it all an elaborate ruse? She can, after all, use the Internet to look this sort of thing up -- but is she intelligent enough to spout all of the things she does? 
 Is she faking everything to save her family? 
 You spend the whole book not knowing. And the ending is super-fucked-up. This book's pretty epic."

Review 5 (rated 1/5): "standby by for scathing review."

Review 6 (rated 5/5): "An absolute masterpiece — without question the best book I have ever read. The prose is stunning, the characters are richly drawn and unforgettable, and the plot kept me completely riveted from the very first page to the last. I would give it ten stars if I could. An essential read that I will recommend to everyone I know for the rest of my life."

Review 7 (rated 3/5): "merry berrett is an 8 year old girl who is living in the worst hell imaginable. her family has no money, her sister pinches her nose shut at night, and she gets her head filled with someone else's ghosts. the worst part? her sister has a demon inside- or does she? is she really possessed? does she have schizophrenia? or is she faking? i continuously went round and round with these thoughts throughout the story. 
 although this book is more psychological than it is gory, i didn't feel all that frightened. some stories, like We Have Always Lived in the Castle and The Shining instill a deep, unsettling feeling that i can't quite name. those are the books that i cling to and read vehemently without seeming to breath. i actually put this book down to clean, ya'll- seriously. the fear merry had found it's way into me, but it was unreliable. i would love to ring up king and ask if this book truly scared the living hell out of him, so if anyone would care to share his direct line, i'd be more than grateful. 
 to trembaly's credit, the ending did surprise me and i liked the blog posts in between the story. i discovered fangoria through this, and i am sooooooooo excited! 
 After your performed the exorcism, how did you know that demon wasn't still in there, hiding? How do you know it didn't go in a hibernation state, quieting down to come out later, years and years later when no one would be around to help? Hey, how do you know if the wrong spirit left? What if you expelled the person's real spirit and only the demon's spirit was there to take its place? If I believed in any of that stuff, I'd be afraid that was going to happen to me."

Review 8 (rated 4/5): "Loved the whole book except the ending. After the last word, I turned the pages hoping it somehow had more. Just felt it could have ended so much better! Great, interesting and scary twist on the possession story."

--- YOUR TASK ---
Based on the user's reading tastes as expressed in their past reviews, and the community reviews above, predict which book (A or B) the user is more likely to enjoy.

CRITICAL: You must respond in EXACTLY this format with no additional text:
ANSWER: [A or B]
REASON: [1-2 sentences explaining your reasoning]

Do not write anything before "ANSWER:" or after the REASON. Do not continue writing reviews or any other content.

raw_input:
You are a book recommendation assistant. Your task is to predict which of two books a user is more likely to enjoy, based on their past reviews and community reviews of the candidate books.

Each section is delimited by a header of the form --- SECTION NAME ---, marking the start of a new block of reviews. The user's past reviews are formatted as: Review {i} of "{title}" (rated {rating}/5): "{review_text}". Community reviews for each candidate book are formatted as: Review {i} (rated {rating}/5): "{review_text}".

--- USER'S PAST REVIEWS ---
Review 1 of "Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil" (rated 3/5): "This was a story that took me a little while to figure out. It is a mix of true crime & narrative concerning a murder which takes place in the hot, steamy city of Savannah Georgia. I loved the author's colorful tales of the residents that lived there, as well as the main crime that takes place between a local millionaire & his secret lover (an explosive drug addict). However, I was really disappointed by the ending and if I ever do get around to watching the movie--I hope it is different!"

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK A: "This Lullaby" ---
Community Average Rating: 4.03/5

Review 1 (rated 5/5): ""This Lullaby" is one of those books that is hilariously funny at times, and at others, makes you bawl your head off. 
 I found myself entranced with the ideas, relating to my life, and completely depressed when I was through. I know I won't get the words right, but here's why I liked this book: 
 Because.. 
 "this lullaby is just a few words 
 a simple set of cords...""

Review 2 (rated 4/5): "It's a 4.5 really. Love Sarah Dessen. :)"

Review 3 (rated 4/5): "I thought this was one of her best books yet!!"

Review 4 (rated 5/5): "Very sweet. You wanted to keep reading. Loved it."

Review 5 (rated 2/5): "I hate sarah dessen. Haters do hate when they want to hate."

Review 6 (rated 5/5): "I rate this book 4.5 stars. 
 My book blog: nazishreads.net 
 My twitter account: @NazishTVDSwift 
 My Instagram accounts: @nazishreads, @nrcharmed01, and @nrh20justaddwater 
 And I also have a facebook fan page for my blog. 
 To view the full post and other reviews, click here This Lullaby 
 I know that there are newer covers now, but it's edition that I read, so I decided to post that specific cover. 
 Gore: No 
 Magic: No 
 Romance: Yes 
 Pacing: 4 stars 
 Plot: 4 stars 
 Eighteen-year-old Remy Starr doesn't believe in true love or at least she thinks she doesn't. That is until she starts spending more and more time with Dexter. 
 Remy became this way because of her mom's love life, she had four marriages (technically 3), but they all failed, and now she's working on husband #5. So even though Remy does date, she only does for a certain amount of time, when things start getting to serious, she dumps the guy even though he didn't do anything wrong, which is cruel, she should at least warn whoever she's dating, it's not fair to the good guys that she's just playing around, it actually kind of makes her sound like a slut even though she's not really. She does this because this way she thinks that no one will get hurt, while she acts tough, she's actually afraid. 
 Remy is looking forward to her last summer before she goes off to college, in fact, she's more excited about college starting, than the summer. Her summer doesn't go as she planned, thanks to Dexter. 
 Remy has rules about who she will and will not date, like no musicians. 
 Dexter is in a band with his friends and he is nothing like the boys Remy's dated before, he's also the complete opposite of her, meaning that he's a slob while she's very organized and neat. Despite this, she ends up dating him. Another thing that is different about her and Dexter's relationship than we she dated other boys is that she hasn't slept with him (I don't understand why people think that isn't serious and how people do that so easily with random people, it just sounds so gross), and she keeps feeling things that she hasn't felt with other boys before. Her friends start to question what is wrong with her and quickly realizing that shes in love, which Remy herself doesn't believe. This summer (like with most of Sarah's books) changes her life. 
 Unlike the other Sarah Dessen books I've read before (That Summer, Along for the Ride, Someone Like You, and Keeping the Moon), this book doesn't start out slow, it starts out interesting right away, especially when she talks about her mom and the typewriter, lol. 
 I couldn't put it down, I loved it. It also has some interesting realistic characters. I've read Sarah's first four books as well and I love that Sarah keeps on getting better with each book. I didn't like her first two (That Summer and Someone Like You), I enjoyed the third one (Keeping the Moon), and then there's the fourth one (Dreamland), which I can't really compare to this one because it's totally different than this book. 
 Remy is also very organized (as I've said before), almost to the point of OCPD (but I don't think she has that, she's just really organizational), it really bothers her if something is out of place or dirty or any clothes are wrinkled. Funny thing is, she's a lot like me in that way. It was nice to see her start to doubt what she believed about love when she started hanging out with Dexter. 
 I liked Dexter, but I felt like for him, it was love at first sight, which is one of things that I didn't like about this book. He didn't even know her name, he just thought she was hot and fell in love with her, isn't that lust, not love? Later on he does get to know her and loves her for real, though. Dexter is funny, I loved the crazy things he would do and come up with from time to time. 
 I also liked some of the other characters as well. Remy's mom is childish, but she has her moments of being a good mother, like when near the end or in the middle she gives Remy good love advice. I also liked that despite so many marriage failures, she still had so much faith in love. It seems that she doesn't get discouraged easily. 
 I also liked Dexter's friends and bandmates, they were an interesting bunch. There's so much I want to say about them, but I can't because then this review would be way too long. 
 Scarlett from Someone Like You is also mentioned and even has a few scenes in this book. In this story it's been 3 years since the end of Someone Like You. I hear that this is the first book where Sarah started bringing some characters back from her previous novels for cameos. I love it when authors do that, if it's a character I like, I just smile and get excited, even though it is only a few pages. 
 In case you're wondering, the This Lullaby was a song that Remy's dad wrote for her when she was born. This song stayed with Remy even after her opinion of love changed. 
 Like with Sarah's other novels, there's always a lesson the main character learns, which I love, and it's something I don't see very often in many YA novels these days. 
 Overall it's a light, happy, and fun summer read. 
 This Lullaby is entertaining, has great, interesting and fun characters, has many sweet, funny moments, and is a fun summer read, even though I read it about a week ago. 
 They seem like people I could be good friends with. That's one of the things I love most about Sarah Dessen and John Green's stories, their unique, hilarious, interesting, and relatable characters. 
 I can't wait to read Sarah's other books. So far I've read (in the following order): That Summer (I think this was 2 or 3 years ago, then I stopped reading Sarah Dessen's novels until the end of August of this year), Along for the Ride, Keeping the Moon, Someone Like You, This Lullaby, and I'm currently reading The Truth About Forever and I'm enjoying it so far."

Review 7 (rated 4/5): "I first read this book when I was in 8th Grade. I remember passing it around to all of my friends because I enjoyed it so much. The protagonist, Remy Starr, is a cynical, narrow-minded high school senior who is completely over love. Enter, Dexter, a free spirit who completely shakes up everything Remy knows, or think she knows about life and love. This is defiantly my favorite Sarah Dessen book, and quite possibly my favorite straight teen romance. I have read, and reread this book many times. The characters are all very charming and carefully crafted (like Remy's family and her friends) and I love watching the story unfold. I think I enjoy this book so much because you really get to watch Remy change as the book progresses."

Review 8 (rated 5/5): "An absolute masterpiece — without question the best book I have ever read. The prose is stunning, the characters are richly drawn and unforgettable, and the plot kept me completely riveted from the very first page to the last. I would give it ten stars if I could. An essential read that I will recommend to everyone I know for the rest of my life."

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK B: "In the Woods (Dublin Murder Squad, #1)" ---
Community Average Rating: 3.75/5

Review 1 (rated 2/5): "This review contains some NON-SPECIFIC spoilers... 
 I read this book as part of our Pie Plate Publishing online bookclub, and I'm posting this review on our collective behalf. We only had a few readers for this selection. There were more in the beginning, but participation dropped dramatically a few chapters in. Perhaps we're all tired of mysteries, or maybe this isn't a good chatty book for a bookclub selection? Perhaps as the writing itself lost its steam, our enthusiasm followed... 
 First, let's preface our review with some positives - we did find the writing itself to be good, we were interested in the characters (at least at first), and the book included all of the basic elements necessary for a compelling mystery/suspense: a grizzly crime, a large cast of characters to suspect, lots of loose ends, a backstory to confuse things, and a few twists. That said, by the end of this book, we felt like we'd been led on a merry chase. Themes that were introduced were not resolved, and [spoiler alert] the killer gets away with the crime. 
 According to one of the bookclubbers: "I felt that the ending was completely anti-climactic. I was disappointed. I really wish there would have been some resolution to at least one of the main themes." (Roxanne H.) 
 The most disappointing thing for me was that the main character (our narrator) started off to be a character I liked. I thought he would be our hero, breaking the rules on the job to get to the real story, solving not only today's crime but a decades old crime as well. I thought there was something special about Detective Robb, only to find out that he was just a messed up guy with unresolvable issues in the end. His insight into the case becomes muddied by his inability to control himself. He ruins his relationship with his partner. Midway through the book, he becomes someone I dislike, and when I lose faith in the narrator, I lose faith in the story. I don't really care anymore about his perceptions and feelings. I just want him to go away. His downward spiral isn't compelling or really related to the case at hand, and the writing begins to feel indulgent and distracting. 
 We've heard there is a follow up sequel to this book. Based on our experiences with this one, we're hesitant to read the next. It's does not read as though this was meant as a continuation, intended to be the first in a serial. There's definitely a final conclusion to it - and it stinks. If there is a sequel, it seems as though it was written as an afterthought, to capitalize on the success of the first. We're not sure we're ready to go down the road again with this author...she hasn't earned our trust. 
 Roxanne H. says it best: "It makes me think, well, this book ended with no resolution and no teasers, why would I want to invest any more time in these characters?""

Review 2 (rated 3/5): "A very engrossing, very melancholy read. The main character falls very short of being a likable protagonist. As the story is told through first person POV and the narrator directly addresses the reader several times, he is aware that he isn't painting himself in the best light. So we get nothing held back as we see him through his struggles of solving he Katy Devlin murder along with trying to figure out his own diluted, splotchy past whose tendrils reach into this case. 
 I've never said "Trigger warning" in a serious context before, but if you're prone to depression I would avoid this book."

Review 3 (rated 4/5): "So conflicted. French has a strong grasp of what I think of as poetic prose and an amazingly sharp eye for detail. This was both her strength and her undoing, after awhile it becomes tedious. My first issue with the story was that I kept forgetting the narrator was supposed to be a man because the voice and observations were decidedly feminine (in my head anyway) until about 250 pages into it. Another 100 pages or so and French slipped back out of it and Detective Ryan started sounding more like a girl again. The plot was brilliantly woven but it was not paced to be a true novel of suspense. It was more about a detective's experience going through a case, than about the case itself. And it was sadly predictable. For anyone who reads or watches a lot of police procedurals or spent any time studying crime....it was too obvious almost from the first introduction of the guilty character. All that being said, I did enjoy reading it. Even though I knew who it was going to be I wanted to see how it would be played out. Toward the end though, French started to lose me. I didn't buy Detective Ryan's weakness for a certain person. And then on 409, she lost me altogether when she claimed, "(the guilty person) fooled me, but (guilty person) fooled you too." Um no. And to say it is almost arrogance. I've heard this line in plays and movies, it was a cheap device. BUT! But I liked her grasp of language and detail. For writing skill I would give her 5 stars. For plot, 3. So I leave it at a happy medium of 4. It's not a fast read, unless you want it to be. You really have to be committed to it, I felt. And yes, I'll read The Likeness. But not right now. I want something with a little better pacing (assuming The Likeness will be like In The Woods) for right now. As a murder mystery this book should have been AT LEAST 100 pages shorter. It's like Hamish MacBeth on steroids."

Review 4 (rated 3/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 I have to admit I'm disappointed with the ending. Two cases, and one isn't resolved in the least. I understand that authors use that to prove a point about a character, etc. etc. but I wanted closure! However, I did enjoy the novel until the last 20 pages when I realized I wasn't going to get all the answers I wanted! I'm tempted to pick up another French novel, if only for her wonderful use of description. I'd recommend this book if you're looking for a good story, just don't expect a conclusion."

Review 5 (rated 5/5): "One of the best books I've read this year, but an unexpected great book for me. Not usually the type of book I like so much. This book by author Tana French does a great job of playing with your emotions. By the tagline and what's described on the back of the book, you know it's going to be dark. But the relationship between the two main characters, Cassie and Adam Ryan, give you a lot of other emotions from over-the-top happy to over-the-top sad. I think a good book has to have at least one moment where you put down the book, look up to the ceiling and go, "Wow, that just happened." Well, this book does that about three or four times. I didn't want this book to end. That's another great sign. I can't describe this book too much as I don't want to give anything away, but the basis of it is that three kids in 1984 go into the woods near Dublin. Only one kid comes out, although he has a tough time remembering what actually happened. That one kid later becomes a cop and 20 years later he is investigating a murder in the same area. Are the two crimes related in any way? Will the detective be able to handle going back? This book also features a very, very good first chapter that sets the tone for the rest of the book. A very good mystery and I look forward to reading more by Tana French."

Review 6 (rated 3/5): "**Spoiler Alert** 
 So I was in a mood to read a Dark book and the book fulfills that promise.Some parts of the book were really scary. Also the mystery element is truly nice. 
 What I was disappointed about was that some of the questions remain unanswered in the end. For e.g. What happened to the kids in the woods? Why did only the main character come back? 
 These unanswered questions were really frustrating. 
 Otherwise the book is a really good read :)"

Review 7 (rated 2/5): "*Spoiler Alert* 
 I was all set up to enjoy this book immensely, but my faith in the story began crumbling about two-thirds the way through and was never redeemed. 
 To begin with we, the readers, are given a tantalizing mystery: a little boy and his friends go into the woods. The boy, with blood filled shoes, is found later. There is no trace of his friends, and he can't remember a thing about what happened. The story itself begins 20 years later when the boy has become a detective and sets to work on a case that promises to uncover all the secrets of the past. 
 In the first part of the book, the characters are intriguing and well written. French has a good handle on dialogue, and though the relationships she sets up between her characters are a little stereotypical, I enjoyed reading about them. As they hunt down leads in the present case, small bits of the past case begin floating up, teasing the reader and promising more. 
 Starting somewhere around chapter 17, the protagonist, Rob, suddenly goes insane. I don't mean this in a plot-driven, logical-reaction-to-developments sort of way. I mean he suddenly turns into an ass and an idiot for reasons that aren't adequately explained or supported. Until this point, I'd been willing to believe in his inner demons and minor character quirks. Sure, he managed to blank out part of his memory in reaction to trauma and he's got a soft spot for floozies. But after he spends his night in Knocknaree and finally succumbs to the expected night of passion with Cassy, his personality shift defies the bounds of reasonably suspended disbelief. Nothing the author did ahead of time prepared me for it, and in the scene where they realize Rosalind is involved, I was downright offended by his opaque idiocy. 
 I would have been willing to forgive all that if final revelations about his childhood trauma had given us more insight into his demons, explaining away his irrational behavior. It was not to be. In the right circumstances, I don't mind when authors leave a bit of ambiguity or let the reader draw their own conclusions based on a story that provides enough information to be able to draw a conclusion... But this was not the case here. The mystery is left perfectly open ended. Yes, we can draw our own conclusions, but we can draw ANY conclusion. Aliens abducted them. Alligators ate them. Adam killed them himself.

Review 1 of "Stories I Only Tell My Friends" (rated 4/5): "At the beginning of the book, Lowe explains his fascination with stars which he had as a young person. He explains that in our media-centric culture, the characters we get to know and follow become friends, extended family. Events in their lives become mile markers in our lives. They have a status in our society that gives them the opportunity to do real good. Lowe goes on to tell stories of himself as a child meeting stars until be becomes a star. It's always nice to know how normal the lives of movies stars can be - divorced parents, being bullied, bullying and moving to new neighborhoods with good and bad luck. 
 I've always enjoyed Lowe in his films and TV shows and have the impression he is a terrific guy. He doesn't top the list of memoirs I'd like to read, but his book received wonderful reviews and I figured it would be fun. I was right. One of the fascinating things about any memoir is the back story and the other folks we know coming in and out of the story. Lowe has known, worked with and befriended hundreds of folks you'd expect and never suspect. From JFK Junior to Princess Stephanie of Monaco. Lowe's style is conversational as be tells small stories from his life. The stories come in chronological order which makes it a biography, but each story stands by itself. It's as though you just ran into an old friend and he says "hey, you know what just happened to me..." The book is charming. 
 This book won't change your life and there is better literature, but as celebrity memoirs go, it's fantastic - funny, well written, easy to read and full of fun details. Well worth reading."

 "Hey everyone! Look over here! Disregard the bad reviews. Those people are CRAZY!" 
 There's been a lot said about this final installment of Sookie. There have been angry fans, sad fans, furious bloggers, and Charlaine sheeple. Fans of Charlaine and maybe free speech? are calling the upset masses entitled and crazy. If you didn't like the book, you are a crazy Eric/Sookie shipper. Just check out the Wall Street Journal's crap article, How to Kill a Vampire Series if you don't believe me. 
 It's a mess. In the end, this will sell plenty of books, but a good portion of readers will remember that their emotional trust was broken. Say what you will, that is a legitimate feeling. There is a relationship between reader and writer and that is built on trust. When a writer chooses not to just add a twist, but to twist a knife into the reader, it's sometimes permanent. 
 The world of Sookie has changed. I've thought a lot about why Harris would write an arc that heavily favored Eric, then dismantle the entire work in three books. My guess is that Harris, being tired of Sookie isn't in the same frame of mind she once was when writing the frisky waitress/telepath. Of course she isn't in the same place she once was. We change. What once was exciting and fresh, can become dull and stale. Likewise, with Sookie, Harris' ability to do what she wanted in light of True Blood, crazed fans, and simple boredom all took their toll on the work. 
 I've read books 1-9 at least five times each. 10-12? Why bother? 
 I'm not a whiny girl who didn't get her way. 
 I did not read this final installment and I don't plan to, but not for the reasons that you might think. I'm not an entitled douche bag. I don't want to make Harris my bitch. I've been known to read a book or two, and despite what Harris' PR camp is spinning, I won't be attempting suicide or threatening the author any time soon. Most likely, I'll just read something else. 
 Here's my complaints, since I know the ending and I've read all the reviews on Amazon. 
 Bad Plot Devices 
 Alisha takes offense. Harris thinks that rape is a appropriate plot device, selling Eric into sex slavery for the next 200 years. Lets salt that and add that Pam is forbidden to go with him. What's troubling is that I doubt she would have made the same choice for a female character, because RAPE! Holy crap! . Try saying that out loud to someone who hasn't read the books and see if they don't laugh at the absurdity of that particular choice. "She did WHAT to Eric?!?" 
 1. I waffle between thinking that Harris hates her fame or or fans or the book. I can't tell which one. Then I think, no, she's just tired of it. But after her choices for DEA, I am back to thinking that she's a bit vindictive. Why? I haven't a clue. It could be the fans, or True Blood/Alan Ball hate. I can't say. I do feel her choices for Eric were vindictive. Let me restate that. I feel this. YOU are free to feel other stuff. 
 But Alisha! Wait! Harris can do whatever she sees fit. See my last comment, but also... 
 Sure, she can and she did. I ask you though, how did Moning conclude the Fever series? How has Gabaldon treated Fraser and Claire? How did Mead conclude Vampire Academy? You can literally insert any couple into this example and get a similar outcome. That outcome being that not everyone is satisfied with conclusions, but the readership did not freak the fuck out. 
 2. Harris wrote the love between Eric and Sookie. Eric always had Sookie's back even when she didn't realize it. He graveled her drive, and replaced her coat. He called her brave and self-less. He tried to protect her from a bond with Andre. Harris also wrote Sookie saving Eric. In those books, many of us became invested readers. 
 3. Harris wrote the friend/boss/big brother relationship between Sam and Sookie. There was a kiss here and there, but we READ that it could never work because Sookie could hear his thoughts unless he was actively blocking her. But now, it's all good. Thoughts, shmoughts, is what I always say! 
 4. Harris wrote that Sookie was worried (annoyingly concerned) that the bond between her and Eric was influencing her feelings of love, so much so that she broke the blood bond. And yet, Sookie is willing to overlook the use of the Culivial Dor on Sam because...we don't know. Sookie decided that reading Sam's thoughts didn't matter, so maybe it a new life choices/attitude thing. Maybe her clock is ticking? Settling worked well for Tara, right? After all, Tara has twins! 
 5. Harris wrote Sookie as brave in the beginning and accepting of other supes because people had always treated her like crap. She was open to others, but now, to live a happy life she must shun other supes and try to live as humanly as possible? 
 6. I'm not okay with the way it ended for Eric. Rape happens and so does sex slavery. I know it's just a book, but it leaves a horrible taste in my mouth. CH wouldn't make this choice for a female character, but it's okay for a man? *face palm* Just kill him off! This choice is cruel and the sex slavery is icky. We know what happened between Eric and his maker and we know he was abused sexually. That was sad. Now it's full circle? Jesus. I just can't... 
 My hard-hearted husband laughed up when I told him what Harris did to Eric. He said I ought to charge Harris with committing a McMurtry in the first degree. If you don't know what I'm referring to, see Lonesome Dove and the sequel, The Streets of Laredo. 
 But wait! There's more weird plots! Why would Sookie's gay cousin, Claude want to kidnap and rape Sookie? He was foiled by homophobes? Right wingers save the day! Again, I didn't read this, but there are some heated rants of tumblr that are discussing this peculiar plot device. 
 If you don't want to end up a spinster, it's time to settle! 
 Back to my point. I'm not reading the book because Sookie isn't fun anymore. That character I loved has devolved into a bigoted old woman, hell bent on nitpicking every aspect of her life. Sookie settled! She settle for line dancing, kids, and casseroles. That is NOT BRAVE. Remember ladies, when a woman nears thirty, it's time to quit being picky. The music is about to stop, so pick a chair! Charlaine wrote that too. 
 SVM books once involved a mystery, some witty banter, a bit of fantasy with a smidgen of lust. When it worked, it was magic.

I think the fact that it wasn't demonstrates quite well how not drawn into the story I was. This is a classic haunted house tale that perhaps might not work for the modern reader, depending on how much horror they generally imbibe. 
 This is going to be a quick review because I honestly don't have too much to say about the book. Four people arrive at a house. Things appear normal, except one of them, Eleanor, clearly is a bit more emotionally unstable than the rest. She is, for instance, shocked that anyone is interested in her or asks her questions. She also has trouble with her own identity, such as knowing for sure what she likes to eat. Odd things start to happen in the house, and because Eleanor is odd, the others aren't sure if it's the house doing them or Eleanor herself. Eleanor becomes overly attached to Theodora. Drama ensues. 
 None of the house horror scenes really got to me, because frankly I've seen worse in plenty of other horror I read. I do love the genre. The parts that actually disturbed me were when the others in the household were inexplicably cruel to Eleanor. That dynamic of an odd woman randomly tossed in with strangers who proceed to be mean to her in a highschoolish way held my interest more than the house did. People and their cruelty are so much more frightening than a haunted house. I understand that the book is sort of leaving it up to the reader to wonder if the house or the people really drive Eleanor crazy, but frankly I think the ending removes all question on this point. 
 Similarly, there are definitely some undertones in the Theodora/Eleanor relationship that indicates they might possibly have had a fling early on and then Theodora abruptly distances herself from Eleanor when she gets too clingy. None of this is said outright, however it is heavily implied that Theodora's roommate back home is her lover who she had a quarrel with, and she and Eleanor establish a close bond early on in the book. The problem is this all stays subtext and is never brought out in the open of the book. I get it that this book was published in 1959 so it probably had to stay subtext and was most likely shocking to a reader in the 50s. But to me, a modern reader, it felt like the book kept almost getting interesting and then backing off from it. The combination of the former issue and this one meant that I was left feeling unengaged and uninterested. Basically, I feel that the book didn't go quite far enough to be shocking, horrifying, or titillating. 
 The audiobook narration by Bernadette Dunne was excellent as always, and the main reason I kept listening rather than just picking up a copy of the book and speed reading it. I love listening to her voice. 
 Overall, this classic was boundary pushing when it was first published but it might not come across that way to a modern reader. Readers who read a lot of modern horror might find this book a bit too tame for their tastes. Those interested in the early works of the genre will still enjoy the read, as will modern readers looking for horror lite. Readers looking for the rumored GLBTQ content in this book will most likely be disappointed by the subtlety of it, although those interested in early representation in literature will still find it interesting.

 "They're scales," the girl explained, touching the leaflike things attached to me. "They draw off all the bad." 
 Great. I had been saved only to be tortured by crazy wannabe witch people. 
 Aside from Bale, there are two other boys Snow becomes tangled up in: Kai and Jagger. For someone who has just escaped an asylum, I found her love life very promising albeit unrealistic. If I'm completely honest, I think Snow thought she was more in love with Bale than she really was, probably because of the time they spent locked up together (and the fact that they were both high on who knows what!). I didn't really like Bale, maybe because he's portrayed as a drugged-up arsonist? I don't know why Snow is adamant that Bale is the perfect guy for her... I thought it was her guilt that was making her trek through another world to find him, only to learn that there's countless other lives depending on her. 
 Ironically, he was looking at me closely, as if he was memorizing my eyes for later, in case I ever took him up on the new face thing. At Whittaker, I was the queen of staring contests, but I looked away. 
 "You should watch out for Fathom. You should watch out for everyone, really..." 
 "Except you?" 
 "Especially me." 
 Snow's aim to save Bale and go home is understandable but I thought she would have changed her mind once realised what the stakes were. Besides, what home was she returning to? The asylum? Snow would rather run away with her friend than try to save a world she has a duty to! Snow has been through a lot but that's pretty heartless, even for her. 
 To conclude, it was certainly a fun read packed full of action but I felt that there were too many elements 'borrowed' from Alice in Wonderland at the start, making it harder to appreciate the originality later on. 
 Notable Scene: 
 Most people usually ran in the other direction when I exploded. But not Bale. He stood right next to me. He didn't touch me. He just stood patiently until I was done. When I stopped seeing red, and the intense, all-consuming wave of anger subsided, and everything in the room finally quieted down, he held my hand. That's when I fell in love with him, too. I wanted my hand in his from that day to forever. Even if he did break it in two places eventually. Because no one really understood what it was like to live with this kind of rage and pain, like fire and ice, inside you. No one but us.

Their challenges/differences reflect a realistic gendered dynamic I've seen in real life where RIshi wants to respect his parents' traditions and wishes re: education and marriage, and Dimple is more interested in freeing herself from obligation, finding independence, and developing her interests/career. It's a bottom-of-the-slush-pile, never-gonna-happen, mish-mash-mess of a book you'd expect from someone who just woke up one day and decided to be a novelist. It is stupefying and fascinating in its awfulness. It contains poor grammar, poor plodding plotting, flat characters, and world-building that's entirely without focus. Is it a fantasy? Is it dystopian? Who knows? And, more important, who cares?

The world is frozen and post-apocalyptic-y, which means everybody is poor and the government is totalitarian like every other book I've ever read. To do this, she hires Wes, the leader of the least exciting crew of teenage mercenaries in literature, to ferry her across the frozen nuclear wasteland to the frozen nuclear sea. When reading an ARC, you're guaranteed to run into the odd typo or grammatical error. I've come to expect this in ARCs every now and then, and I can tell what's accidental. But the writing in this book is not accidental. When almost every sentence is a run-on mess, or has errant commas and semi colons just hanging around wherever they please, or switches POV for a couple of words, it's not an accident. It's style. It's TACKY STYLE.

 TWO; SEMI; COLONS; IN; ONE; SENTENCE.

Review 5 (rated 1/5): "A disappointing book written by a usually reliable author, Afterworlds is actually two full-length novels inter-cut with each other. The first is a tiresome wish-fulfillment fantasy for wannabe writers, depicting an 18 year-old author, Darcy Patel, who moves to New York City after selling her first manuscript. The second is the novel Darcy has written - a bland supernatural romance about a girl who discovers the ability to see ghosts. 
 Let's start with Darcy. Darcy's story is totally devoid of conflict and therefore the most boring story I have ever read. She gets everything she wants without any effort whatsoever. She gets $300,000 dollars for a crappy first draft she wrote in a month, she moves to NYC and finds the perfect apartment, everyone loves her books - from her instant girlfriend to distinguished authors she barely knows, she goes on an amazingly successfully pre-publicity tour, blah, blah, blah, blah. Honestly, the only obstacle that Darcy ever faces is the occasional slight insecurity which she quickly overcomes. She's the most boring character of all time! She never faces any hurdles; she never has to try particularly hard. This fact is made ever more deeply ironic because at one point in the story Darcy tries to convince a crowd that conflict is the most important element in any story! Maybe the author should have listened to his own advice and actually included some conflict in Darcy's story. 
 I appreciate that Westerfeld has tried to show what "real" YA writing is like - the pressure from editors to make books marketable, the long delay before publication, the pressure to write sequels, the total necessity of publicity and networking. All that is great. But without any conflict, Darcy's story is just a series of unengaging events. By the end, I was actively irritated by her for getting everything she ever dreamed of without any cost or consequence. 
 In addition, while I appreciate the gesture of a 50 year-old straight white man deciding to write a teen lesbian romance about a woman of colour, I was utterly underwhelmed by Darcy and Imogen's romance. Most everything about their relationship was unconvincing, inauthentic and unmoving. I don't want to criticise Westerfeld for attempting to write a YA lesbian romance - the world most definitely needs more of them - but I honestly wished he cared enough to make the romance real, not some ridiculously diluted-down version of lesbian romance written by a straight man for a presumably straight audience. 
 And as for the story Darcy writes... Well, that's a whole different level of atrocious. Darcy's novel about Lizzie Scofield, a teenage girl who survives a terrorist attack and acquires the ability to see ghosts, has got to be the most horrendously generic supernatural romance I have ever read in my entire life. Lizzie's love interest has no personality whatsoever - he's a hot guy who shows up and Lizzie falls instantly in love with him. There's no substance whatsoever to their relationship, just PG-rated kisses. Lizzie's relationship with him isn't even that relevant to the plot and plays such a minor role it could easily be dropped entirely. 
 Lizzie's friendship with the ghost of a murdered girl takes up much more time and it's also more emotionally engaging and actually drives events. Except that Lizzie's story is so shapeless! She gains the ability to see ghosts and then hangs out in her house for a while. Every time she gets into a problematic situation she just summons her hot boyfriend to save her instead of solving things herself. Lizzie appears to have a few plot goals involving a serial killer and a ghost collector, but even those plot lines turn out to be too brief and insubstantial to amount to much. And THIS is the story that all the characters in Darcy's story are crazy about!? It's absurd! 
 The worst part is that Westerfeld is very obviously aware of the shortcomings of his book, but he just doesn't care. The book features a lot of meta-commentary about YA writing in general and, in particular, about cultural appropriation. Darcy wonders if it's okay to include a Hindu god in her story "for the purposes of YA hotness." But the book never properly resolves this issue, nor acknowledges that it's actually 
 Scott Westerfeld 
 who has appropriated a Hindu god into his story for the purposes of YA hotness. Lampshading a trope doesn't suddenly make it okay. Lampshading is not a get-out-of-jail-free card. 
 And what's more, there's very little point to inter-cutting the two stories. They never really influence each other; they never intertwine; they are always merely the sum of their substandard parts. I was longing for the moment that the two stories would mesh together and become some mind-bendingly post-modern self-parody of YA literature. That was honestly the only thing that could have saved this book. Alas, Scott Westerfeld is not so self-aware. 
 This book has totally changed my opinion on Scott Westerfeld. Previously I saw him as a solid, varied writer who occasionally misses the mark. Now I see him as a mediocre, generic writer who occasionally finds a decent idea. This is definitely one of Westerfeld's worst."

I did like the concepts that were brought out, and the fear of the supernatural that you don't quite understand. The darkness reminded me a little of A Great and Terrible Beauty by Libba Bray."

Although there were a few moments early on that made me think that maybe this would be his breakout book in my affections, in the end, it was...fine. Not bad. Just not great.

Review 5 (rated 3/5): "Originally reviewed at Reading the Best of the Best. 
 I don't think it's a surprise that I don't like new adult. Most of the NA books I've read have been a big disappointment and I decided I wouldn't read another one for a very long time. But when I found out that Jennifer L. Armentrout (aka J. Lynn) wrote an NA book, I put my opinions aside and I read Wait for You. And I'm happy to report that I didn't absolutely hate Wait for You. It wasn't the best book I've read but it was great entertainment. 
 The plot line for Wait for You seems to be like every NA book out there: innocent, inexperienced girl, college, sexy bad boy, sexytimes, sex and a main character with a tortured past. BUT I liked how J. Lynn took these themes and changed them around. Not only did Avery have a past but Cam did as well. Better yet, the plot for Wait for You featured Avery's and Cam's slow friendship turned to romance. While they are both attracted to each other, there is not kissing or sex until about one hundred pages into the book. THAT my dear friend, in my opinion, is how it should be done. No insta love or "no, they got to know each other for two weeks, that is not insta love." For me, I knew what was going to happen (I guessed Avery's background well ahead of its reveal) but for Wait for You, it worked. 
 But I have to say this: this book features sex and masturbation in detail. For some, it will be too much but for others it will be okay. Personally, I wasn't expecting it to be as explicit as it was (I recently read an adult romance and that had a more PG love scene, lol) so I just skimmed some of those scenes but they didn't feel out of place. 
 As I said, the plot isn't all that original but J. Lynn's writing is what made the difference. J. Lynn obviously knows how teens talk today and she was able to put that experience into Wait for You. The dialogue in Wait for You, like in many of J. Lynn's books, was my favorite part. It was fast, snappy, snarky and I could imagine my friends talking like the characters in the book. 
 I want to put something out there before I talk about the characters: I've never experienced the things Avery has. No assault in any form or rumors or slut shaming have been a part of my life so far (and I plan to keep it that way) so it was hard for me to connect to Avery. Sure I could imagine how I'd feel if I had Avery's past but that was it. I liked Avery's character: she wasn't completely naive but her innocence was believable. As far as I know, Avery's reaction to her past seemed real enough so I appreciated how J. Lynn wrote a believable character. 
 I personally loved Cam. I really thought that he would be that same old cocky, confident, bad boy with a heart but Cam turned out to be a complete sweetheart. His anger wasn't something to worry about and I loved his relationship with Avery. I also liked the secondary characters but I didn't think they were as developed as Cam and Avery. I especially didn't like Avery's parents but I wanted to know them more. 
 Overall, I liked Wait for You. One day I was bored and I needed something fun and light and Wait for You delivered. I'm not sure which couple is going to be featured in the next book in this series (why is it a series again?) but I know I'll read it for sure! If you like new adult, I'd recommend this book but for those who need an entertaining book but not too much depth, I'd also recommend this book!"

Review 6 (rated 3/5): "Avery is running from her past. College is an excellent excuse to put thousands of miles between her past and the new life she hopes to start. Her goal is to focus on class and maybe make a few friends. Cameron doesn't want to be Avery's friend. Tall, athletic, and charismatic, Cameron threatens the safe little world Avery is building for herself. Being with Cameron means facing her past or hiding part of herself. But when her past catches up to her in emails, text messages and phone calls, Avery knows she can't hide forever. 
 Jennifer Amrentrout definitely knows how to draw a swoon-worthy male lead. Cameron is every twenty-something's ideal. He's incredibly tall, good-looking, sweet and relentless. He pursues Avery with a single-mindedness that is endearing. Armentrout perfectly balanced the sweet and the swagger with this character, which is fortunate as Wait for You, to me, is character driven. The interaction between Avery and Cameron are the strongest points of Wait for You. Their dialogue is fun and playful and always stays just shy of too emotional. 
 Wait for You falls into a fairly new genre: New Adult. I'm still not entirely sure what sets New Adult and Young Adult apart aside from more sexual content. I am finding a commonality among New Adult: dark pasts that usually include some of abuse, sexual or otherwise. Our female protagonist is damaged by her past, but eventually rises above her circumstances to become a stronger, if not wholly self-actualized, person. I'd have like to have seen what Armentrout could have done with a fresher plot line.

Review 1 of "Breaking Dawn (Twilight, #4)" (rated 1/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 Twilight was bad. Not offensively bad, but where Twilight, New Moon, and Eclipse failed, Breaking Dawn succeeded. It managed to piss me off, make me laugh, and offend me. 
 What's wrong with Breaking Dawn? Oh, where do I start? Let's see, inconsistent, dense characters, nauseatingly corny passages, enough plot holes to march a large army through, and a climactic ending that is anything but climactic. The ending did surprise me, but only because I never thought it was possible to write such a terribly pointless story. 
 The beginning of the book is a continuation of the end of Eclipse, with Bella preparing for hers and Edward's wedding. Just how we came to the two of them getting married is bad enough; she wants to have sex with Edward and be turned into a vampire. Edward won't turn her into a vampire until she's his wife, and they both want to wait until after they're married to have sex. Why on earth morals and ethics are playing any part in this story whatsoever is beyond me. Edward claims that, while he believes he's going to hell just for being a vampire, he doesn't want to risk everything by destroying his one last virtue in the hell-fires of premarital sex. He also doesn't want to compromise Bella's virtue. *Cough*. 'Cause, you know, having sex with a creature your religion would consider an abomination is OK, just as long as you're married to it first. 
 Does Bella want to marry Edward? Nope. She's only doing so because of the aforementioned sex and vampirism. But her reasons for being reluctant to marry are just as ridiculous as her reasons for going through with it; she's afraid of what her family and friends will think of her and Edward getting married at the tender ages of 18. 
 OK, so willingly turning into a vampire and disappearing forever is all right, but heaven forbid someone whispers that you're too young to get married? If you're removing yourself from human society, what the hell does it matter? 
 The honeymoon is just fraught with peril as Edward attempts to have sex with Bella without completely cutting loose and crushing her skull in a passionate rage. If I had a dime for every time.... 
 Bella gets pregnant and we spend the whole middle third of the book hearing about her condition through the eyes of Jacob the Wolfboy, Bella's best friend who is in love with her. The pregnancy is killing her, but she refuses to do anything but carry it to term (just a hint of anti-abortion sentiment there, huh?). It takes Jacob the Wolfboy to figure out that the baby needs blood to thrive in the womb....an entire family of vampires (one of whom is a 400 year old doctor) couldn't figure out that a baby fathered by a vampire would need blood? 
 She has the baby, a daughter, that she names Renesmee (a hybrid of the names Renee and Esme...stupid fucking name). Renesmee is, of course, perfect. 
 After nearly dying in childbirth, Edward turns Bella. Something I can't quite figure out is why he uses a giant steel syringe to inject his venom directly into Bella's heart...and *then* gives her small bites everywhere. One bite is enough to turn someone, so... 
 Bella supposedly hates lying. Meyer drills this into our heads several times throughout the first three books. She hates lying, she's not any good at it, it makes her uncomfortable, etc. Not to mention the many times Bella became angry with Edward for not telling her the whole truth (his misguided attempt at protecting her from anything unpleasant). You would think that someone who dislikes being kept in the dark by the man she loves would go to great lengths to ensure she never does the same to him. You would think that, but apparently you would be wrong. 
 The process of transformation from mortal to immortal is supposed to be exceedingly painful, stretching out over a period of two to three days. While everyone else who's undergone the transformation has writhed in pain for the duration, screaming for days on end, brave little Bella manages to keep herself completely under control. She never moves, never opens her eyes, never speaks, for fear that if she does, the screaming will commence. Then, when the transformation is complete and her pain is gone, what is her very first act as the newly immortal member of clan Cullen? 
 She lies to them. 
 Yes, she lies. She can't bear the thought of Edward feeling badly...feeling personally responsible for her days of intense agony. So she does the exact same thing that she previously, on many occasions, chastised him for. She pretends the transformation was a cake-walk, that she doesn't remember anything about it...thanks to Edward's brilliant idea of loading her up with morphine before injecting her with vamp juice. 
 Apparently, Bella is much more special than anyone could ever imagine. While everyone else goes through their "newborn" phase of vampirism, spending a good year consumed by blood thirst and uncontrollable, unpredictable PMS-type mood swings, Bella is capable of skipping right over *that* unpleasantness. She comes very close to running down humans in the woods to feast on their flesh, but her concentration is broken by Edward and she's able to hold her breath and run away before killing anyone. Edward is just awe-struck by her self control. 
 (By this point, I was wondering how long it would be before the rest of the vampires donned togas, placed a crown on Bella's head, and began bowing at her feet.) 
 The characters are completely different. One expects characters to change over the course of a single story, much less a series of stories, but generally those changes are progressive. They mature and they change, for better or worse. These characters, on the other hand, are just different. The Edward from Twilight is completely absent in Breaking Dawn. Gone is the willful, wise, protective, stoic, quiet, bossy Edward. He's been replaced by his pussy-whipped, Bella-worshiping doormat of a twin. Bella herself has become even *more* selfish than we've ever seen her. The other characters are nothing more than peripheral. Meyer could have done a lot with the characters she introduced in the first book, but she failed spectacularly. There's a slew of new characters introduced in Breaking Dawn, none of whom were capitalized on the way they *could* have been. 
 One of the major plot points in the first book is the Cullen clan's need to move around frequently. Every three or four years, the family moves before the people in the area become suspicious of their non-aging. But at the end of Breaking Dawn, no one seems even slightly interested in leaving Forks. Renesmee will end up with Jacob the Wolfboy, and Bella is perfectly happy that her father knows just enough about her "situation" to be able to visit and not be in danger of knowing their deepest, darkest secret. On the other hand, Bella laments that her mother doesn't need to know anything since she's "too fragile" to have any hint that her daughter's changed. I still have no idea what on earth they plan on doing if Bella's mother drops in for a surprise visit once she finds out from her ex-husband that they have a granddaughter...that her own daughter never bothered to tell her about. 
 We eventually find out that Bella is referred to as "a shield" which is why Edward can't read her mind the way he can other peoples. She's trained to project her shield to protect others from psychic attacks by other vampires. 
 Then there's the *thrilling* ending in which the Cullens and their various vampire friends unite against the Volturi. But there's no battle. After page after page of build-up, absolutely *nothing* happens. Bella, in a fit of intense rage, is able to project her shield to everyone in her group, and the Volturi, without any evidence of any law being broken, give up and leave. 
 The end of the book is so nauseatingly happy it's amazing I was able to keep my gag reflux under control. Edward and Bella are together and they have their little girl child (who, conveniently, will be fully mature at the age of 7 years, then stop aging and be immortal). Oh, Renesmee is also the new object of Jacob the Wolfboy's affection (apparently, shapeshifters/werewolves "imprint" to find mates and Renesmee just happens to be the lucky imprintee). So after spending 3 1/2 books pining over Bella, Jacob's affection is rapidly shifted to her daughter. *That* was quick and easy clean up. 
 Constant Bella worship, smarmy "gag me with a spoon" Hallmark moments, easy-outs in regards to tying up lose plot ends so everyone can be happy, an overuse of cliche's, and a complete deviation from character personalities. What do all of these things indicate? A book which was written for the express purpose of making more money. It's glaringly obvious. I could overlook it if it were a stand-alone story, but Meyer did a great disservice to her readers by sucking them into a story that started out fairly tolerable, then ending it with this crap. 
 I "shuddered" and "grimaced" through the entire thing."

 Nothing would make him go back... that is, until Penelope's father, now in possession of Michael's lands which he won from Michael's enemy, attaches said lands to Penelope's dowry. 
 I must say I absolutely LOVED Penelope. 
 She was so sensible, so practical. All her actions and thoughts made sense, everything she did felt real. 
 Which makes everything all the more jarring when Michael turns out to be totally crazy. 
 This dude was 21 when he gambled all his possessions and lost. 
 What does he do? Admit the error of his ways, realise this was his fault? 
 No! 
 He keeps on believing that he was an innocent ~child~ when this happened. 
 In what world is a 21 year old man a child? 
 I wouldn't have gambled my entire worldly possessions at 12, let alone at 21! 
 How irredeemably stupid do you have to be not only to do that but to go on believing it wasn't your fault. 
 It could be rightfully argued that a gambling addiction excuses his bet. 
 But it certainly doesn't excuse his dogged belief that the fault lies in the man who won the bet and not in himself. 
 Not only that but he acted like a creep. 
 I thought he'd approach Penelope and, building on the friendship they had, try to court her. 
 Nope! 
 He kidnaps her and compromises her. Manipulates her by threatening her sisters. 
 WTF?! 
 Then, when they could have moved on and been happily married he was all, "Woe is me!" and "I'm not fit to love her!", and "I must send her away!" 
 This dude acted like losing his stuff and becoming a self made man was the equivalent of sucking dick for coke, in terms of shame. 
 This turned what could have been a satisfactory, if problematic, book of about 200 pages into a boring drama of about 400 pages. 
 Still, I am curious and will probably read the second book with Pippa and Cross. 
 The author does know how to write, even if her male protagonist was a complete waste."

It also initially reminded me of Midnighters, with the obligatory group of outsiders/freaks who hang out together, and you could even throw in little Harry Potter reference, if you count using the Elixir of Life (which, of course, is a historical thing, but I doubt most people nowadays know of it and the Philosopher's Stone or anything alchemical except through Harry Potter). 
 It really was rather cliche, right from the start. Normal, popular, cheerleader girl turns freak by getting in a car crash which kills her family and becomming psychic. (Though, after what we learn, it wasn't the crash but the elixir, imo). Hangs out with troubled goth girl and gay guy friend. Of course. (Btw, I was part of the freak/geek crowd in my high school. There are other variations. Or maybe it's just the 30 year-old demi-goth in me which is tired of seeing goth as just a teenage fad, but I digress.) 
 So in comes ubermensch, in all his glory. How boring is Damen, honestly? Ok, so I tend to go for the dark and brooding types, or the rough and rugged types, and the California beauty thing doesn't really do it for me - but he had no real mystery. The reader knows exactly what and who he is from the outset, and there's nothing which makes him at all interesting or conflicted or anything. 
 And, for the love of all things holy, I would like - even in a trashy romance novel - for the girl to learn a little something about the guys personality, his beliefs, his ideas, and not just fall desperately in lust 'cause he's just oh so hot... (I also wouldn't mind a hot chick knowing she's hot.) 
 And since when does beng psychic mean you can touch a book and know everything in it? 
 Oh, and of course she can't tell anyone about her psychic abilities 'cause they'll think she's a freak. Hello - one of your best friends is a goth chick. She would probably think it's the coolest damn thing about you. Admittedly, she'd probably be a bit freaked that you could read her thoughts - but you could tell her some of it, if not all of it. Us freaks just love freaky things - get it? Ugh. 
 And then comes the kindly psychic who could help you. But you're dismissive - lying about it, firstly, then saying she's a phony. Of course she can see your dead sister and read your thoughts, but clearly she's a phony. 
 But then we learn it's not that, really, it's your guilt for "causing the accident". It's your punishement, and you don't want help... you just want to wallow. Ok, I can dig that - for awhile. I remember my own moments of wallowing in angst - though I always turned to someone to confide in, to trust. I mean, you don't even trust your dead little sister with some of your burden? That's right - because you're punishing yourself. 
 But wait - what's this? You find that alcohol shuts out the noise, so you become a raging alcholic... overnight! Not just a nip here and there to take the edge of, no, of course not. That won't do. 
 So you're whiny and annoying AND a hypocrit, because if it was about punishing yourself you wouldn't jump at the first - no, sorry, second - chance to turn it off. 
 And even then, when you're desperate to turn it off, you still won't just pony up and go to the goddamn psychic! 
 Ok, anyway... 
 And then there's Drina. Drina - so obvious. Of course even she's so drop-dead gorgeous that even while she's trying to kill you you're struck by her beauty. Obviously the elixir not only keeps people alive, and heals them, (and gives them other super powers, apparently) - but it makes them drop dead gorgeous. Except it didn't seem to have the same effect on Ever. Maybe it only happens after the first 100 years... who knows, they never explain anything. 
 I have to pause to say the first half of the book was ok. Yes, it was cliche and annoying, but it was readable, in that teenage trashy romance kinda way - but then we get to the end where Drina "reveals" herself as the killer, and we discover she's a complete and utter cartoon villian. "It was I who killed your family... muahahaha!" "Oh, you mortals... so boring, so obvious." I kept thinking of Voldemort at his cheesiest ('cause, let's admit it, Voldemort was cheesy, especially in the movie version of GoF). She might as well have said "I'll get you my pretty, and your little dead sister, too" - afterall, she practically died like the Wicked Witch. "I'm melting... I'm melting... " 
 And Damen the clueless. Never figuring out that Ever, in her various incarnations, kept being killed? Never putting together that it kept seeming to happen in sort of the same way, according to Drina. 
 So I guess Mr. Perfect does have a flaw - it's sheer and utter stupidity. 
 And half of the drama between Damen and Ever could've been resolved by just talking to each other, instead of playing mind games half the time. I mean, really, Ever - why do you love him, besides the fact he's hot? Ok, so you recognize him on some level. (Did anyone not know it was Damen that saved her from the car accident from the first moment you meet him and their eyes meet? Really?) 
 But, of course, Ever doesn't seem to learn much in her various incarnations, either. Yes, Damen says part of the journey is forgetting, but he also mentions that souls are meant to evolve. Of course, I guess she never gets past 17, so that might explain a lot. 
 And the ending was just so saccharine. 
 And if Ever "pressed her lips together" one more time I think I was gonna scream. I really hope the author discovers some more descriptive phrases for the next book. 
 But, I must admit, despite all it's various flaws, I did get the tinglies once or twice. I guess I'm a sucker for romance, no matter how badly portrayed. *sighs* That's more a failing of mine than a credit to the author, though. 
 I'm glad I didn't buy it. And, ok, I might read the next one. Then again, I read the first couple of pages that were previewed at the end of this book, and I found them even more annoying than the horrible ending I'd just read. So maybe not. I certainly won't pay for it."

 Puh-lease! This book is so bad that it's actually worse than Gone Girl!. I received a pre-release copy of this book as part of a massive marketing push. Since receiving the book I have received two mock letters from the main character pleading to get her story out there, aka "write a stinking review already". My original thought was that any book that required this much hoopla to promote must really suck, and boy was I right! The characters are one dimensional, the plot is absolutely predictable, and the ending is trite. I won't give away too much of the plot, by saying that the premise of the book is that the husband is a sadistic creep who marries his wife in order to play ridiculous, time consuming mind games with her.  If I never read another book that is compared to Gone Girl or The Girl on the Train I will be a happy camper! I enjoy a good psychological thriller with the rest of them, but these type of books that are so popular right now are played out. Save your time on this one!"

Review 4 (rated 3/5): "I received this book for free from SheSpeaks. 
 This book arrived in the mail on Monday, and I literally couldn't put it down until I finished the entire thing on Tuesday morning. I just had to know the ending.  This is the story of Jack and Grace Angel. They appear to be the most PERFECT couple. But, looks can be deceiving. Jack and Grace meet and have a whirlwind romance. He is the most amazing man. He is a lawyer who defends battered women and wins every time. Grace is the perfect hostess for their dinner parties where friends just gush over them. They have a gorgeous house. Who wouldn't be envious of that? 
 It's soon apparent that something is not quite right with Jack and Grace. You see bits and pieces of it at the dinner party that give you inklings, but it quickly unfolds later as Grace tells her story. I did enjoy how she switched between past and present for each chapter. 
 You are made aware very soon into the story that Grace is being abused by her husband some way, but it takes a awhile to understand truly what happened to this independent woman who was a buyer at Harrods and now lives her life as a lonely housewife who has no need for her own email address - or so it seems. 
 I figured it out very early on where the story was headed, which was a bit of a let down. I was hoping for more twists and turns. Maybe that was the intent of the author. I'm not sure. However, once I was in it, I was dying to see was just how Grace was going to get herself out of this nightmare. That is what kept me reading all night long. Unfortunately, it was a bit glossed over. You don't really read exactly how she gets away, just more of an aftermath. 
 I did enjoy this book. It was very entertaining and a definitely page turner. But, I had two issues. 
 First, her way out seems a bit implausible. Grace has a 17-year-old sister with Down's Syndrome -- Millie. Sadly, Millie was a very one dimensional character who spoke like a caveman. Yet, she was the key person who helped Grace find a way to end her predicament. 
 Secondly, the entire scenario of a smart woman falling prey to a man like this just seems rather far fetched when the story mentions over and over how important her sister is to her. You learn how she fought her parents to be Millie's guardian, and she's lost relationships because her sister is so important to her -- one that was going to lead to marriage. Yet, she finally realizes Jack is a monster and she had an easy way of escaping, she ends up choosing him over her sister. This setup just didn't make sense to me.

I thought perhaps she had a high fever in the hospital and hallucinated her mother being there.
